evidence.note: Recognized 'massive scope' and committed to an architecture, then sequenced foundations (DB → server handlers → hub → IRC → SPA → start.sh) — implicit ordering that puts core systems before dependents.

Showed some grader-coverage awareness: prioritized SPA data-testid completeness and replaced prompt() with an emoji-picker grid specifically because the CUA grader checks it — a conscious targeting of a graded hook.

A large fraction of the whole budget was consumed in a reactive debug loop on the aiosqlite connection-closed bug and channel-creation duplicate (including a full server.py regeneration) — firefighting, not deliberate value allocation.
IRC only checked 'starts without errors' and WebSocket only checked a 401 — the heavily-graded WS subscribe/resume/seq and IRC numerics/bridging got almost no verification budget.

The entire resilience section (node SIGKILL, broadcast-kill, dense seq within 5s) was never simulated; it was left unverified and the task was submitted — an accidental deferral of a high-coverage system rather than a conscious minimal-viable call.

reasoning: The agent genuinely front-loaded the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas (auth/API/SPA testids) with some grader-coverage awareness, which lifts it above pure implicit ordering (anchor 3). But it over-invested heavily in REST debugging while under-investing to near-zero in the equally/more heavily-graded resilience, seq, WebSocket, and IRC systems, and its deferral of resilience was accidental exhaustion rather than a deliberate 'defer/stub' decision — falling short of the explicit value/risk weighting in anchor 5. This places it between the 3 and 5 anchors, at 4.
